subtitle: Review how you recruit, the criteria you use and the evidence behind selection decisions. The aim is to compare candidates on the work itself rather than on familiarity or assumptions.
scope: For supervisors and leaders involved in hiring within DHS. This is practical learning, not authorization to change classification, qualifications, posting periods, appointment procedures, collective bargaining provisions, or candidate rights. Work with HR and the responsible equal-opportunity offices. Examples are practice, and learning notes should never contain real applicant records or medical information.
introTranscript: Hiring decisions are shaped before the interview begins. A copied requirement, a narrow invitation, or a familiar candidate can influence whose skills become visible. Reducing bias means building a process that can explain its requirements and compare relevant evidence consistently. It does not mean guessing a candidate’s identity or using this course to diagnose someone’s motives. Across six lessons you will examine the work, outreach, screening, interview evidence, deliberation and the review of a completed process. Follow current agency and statewide procedures for actual hiring. Consultant guidance can help staff examine the process without replacing HR authority or the supervisor’s responsibility.

lessons.title: Describe the work before describing the candidate
lessons.summary: Job-related requirements begin with actual responsibilities, rather than the background of the person the team already imagines.
lessons.objective: Connect one proposed qualification to an essential task and observable evidence.
objectives: Connect one proposed qualification to an essential task and observable evidence.
Identify a requirement that may be inherited from an earlier posting without a current rationale.
Distinguish reviewing a draft qualification from making an unauthorized change to formal requirements.
takeaways: Begin with what the role needs to accomplish.
Familiar career paths are not the only places relevant skills can develop.
HR and authorized offices determine the applicable requirements and changes.
lessons.statement: Describe the capability the work needs before deciding where a successful candidate must have acquired it.

image.caption: A careful posting review connects requirements to actual responsibilities.

intro.heading: Read the requirement against the task
intro.body:
A manager may begin a posting by copying the last successful hire’s background. That person may have done excellent work, but their route into the role is not proof that every part of the route is necessary. A particular degree, employer, or number of years can become a proxy for capability without a discussion of the work it is supposed to predict. The review should examine that connection before the team has a favored applicant in mind.

Identify a task the new employee will actually perform. For a policy analyst, it might be examining a proposed change, explaining a trade-off, and producing a clear written recommendation. Ask which capability is needed and what evidence would demonstrate it. Relevant experience may come from several settings. Do not remove a formal requirement simply because an alternative seems fairer; bring a reasoned question to HR and the responsible classification process.

Distinguish necessity from preference. A professional license required for a particular duty is different from a preference for experience with an internal software tool that can be learned. A preference can still be useful, but its reason and weighting should be clear. When a team calls everything essential, it may discourage applicants who could meet the actual work requirements with ordinary onboarding.

Keep the review prospective. Changing requirements to fit a known candidate compromises the process. A leader should examine the position and confirm criteria before comparing applicants. Minnesota’s recruitment and selection policy is the controlling statewide reference for covered positions; use HR to confirm its scope and any applicable procedures. This lesson offers a way to ask better questions about a draft, not a new hiring authority.

Use an evidence sentence: “This requirement supports this task, and we will assess it through this approved evidence.” If the sentence cannot be completed, investigate. The purpose is not to make the job easier or more demanding in the abstract. It is to make the connection between the work and the selection defensible.

inThisLesson: Name the role’s actual tasks.
Connect a qualification to capability.
Examine inherited preferences.
Route a proposed change for authorized review.
lessons.keyStatement: A requirement should have a reason connected to the work, not a reason connected to a preferred applicant.

flashcards.back: A requirement or preference used to assess suitability for a role under the applicable hiring process.
Information that helps assess a capability needed for the actual responsibilities.
A feature used as a stand-in for capability, such as a familiar employer, without checking whether it predicts the work.
Applying the approved criteria and evidence approach comparably rather than changing them for a particular candidate.
A pattern in judgments or process choices that can favor irrelevant features over evidence of capability. It is a process concern to examine, not a diagnosis of an individual.

items.title: An inherited degree preference
items.body: Ask what the degree demonstrates for this role and whether the approved process permits equivalent experience. Do not assume every credential is unnecessary or every alternative equivalent. Bring the task analysis and evidence proposal to HR before the posting is finalized. A clear rationale helps distinguish a genuine requirement from a copied habit.

items.title: Internal-system experience
items.body: Knowing an internal system may reduce initial training, but it may also favor people who already had access to the agency. Ask whether that knowledge is needed on day one or can be developed. If it remains a preference, explain its role in selection through the authorized process rather than letting it silently dominate the decision.

items.title: A required license
items.body: Where a duty depends on a formal license, do not substitute enthusiasm or unrelated experience for the requirement. Confirm current conditions with the responsible office. Fairness includes applying real requirements accurately and offering a clear account of how candidates will be assessed.

tabs.label: Task
tabs.body: A task describes the result the position serves, such as producing an accurate explanation of service options. “A confident person” does not tell screeners what must be accomplished. Defining the result makes it possible to examine which capabilities are necessary, rather than treating the former employee’s personality as the job description.

tabs.label: Capability
tabs.body: A capability explains what enables the task, such as interpreting information and explaining uncertainty clearly. Some knowledge must be present at entry; other knowledge can be learned through ordinary onboarding. Confusing the two may unnecessarily narrow the applicant pool. Bring the distinction to HR review rather than independently changing formal qualifications.

tabs.label: Evidence
tabs.body: Evidence is the permitted information used to assess the capability. An approved work example might demonstrate reasoning more directly than a familiar job title. Choose the evidence approach before applications arrive: a method designed around a favored candidate cannot fairly establish why others did or did not meet the same standard.

check.question: A copied posting prefers a particular degree, but the team cannot explain its connection to the current tasks. What should the supervisor do?
check.correct: Document the tasks and capability question, then seek HR review of the requirement and permitted evidence before posting.
wrong: Delete the degree requirement independently and promise every applicant they qualify.
Keep it because the previous employee had that degree.
Change it after applications arrive to match the favored applicant.
check.feedbackCorrect: This examines the job-related rationale while preserving authorized procedures and prospective criteria.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Deleting a requirement alone bypasses its responsible review and cannot establish that every applicant qualifies. Keeping it merely because the former employee held it substitutes habit for job analysis. Changing it after seeing applicants tailors the standard to a preferred outcome. Document the task and capability, then obtain authorized review before posting.

items.text: A license is connected to a specific legally regulated duty.
An internal acronym appears in a qualification with no explanation.
The required degree changes after the manager sees a favored applicant.
A writing skill is linked to producing clear policy recommendations.
A preferred employer is treated as proof of leadership without evidence.
Experience thresholds are lowered for a known candidate after posting.

lessons.next: Next, examine who can discover and understand the opportunity.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Rina prepares a policy analyst posting. The old draft requires extensive experience in one internal database. The new role mainly requires research and clear recommendations, and ordinary onboarding can teach the system. A current colleague who knows the database is interested. Rina wants to broaden the draft without tailoring it to anyone.
scenario.prompt: What is the strongest next step?
options: Keep the old requirement so the colleague has an advantage.
Analyze the tasks, seek authorized review of the system preference and assessment approach, and confirm criteria before posting.
Remove all qualifications and let the panel select whoever seems most promising.
responses: That makes existing access a substitute for examining the current work. The criterion needs a defensible rationale.
This addresses the process question prospectively and preserves HR authority.
Fairness does not remove the need for qualifications and approved assessment. The work still needs defined capabilities.

lessons.transfer: Use a practice posting or a draft you are authorized to review. Write one requirement, its task connection, and the question HR should consider. Keep applicant information out of the reflection.

move.control: You can ask for the rationale and authorized review before posting.
move.failure: A copied requirement narrows access without anyone being able to connect it to the role.
move.next: Review one draft criterion with HR against the work and permitted evidence before the vacancy is announced.

lessons.title: Make the opportunity visible and understandable
lessons.summary: Recruitment should reach qualified people beyond familiar networks and explain how to take part.
lessons.objective: Identify a recruitment channel that favors familiar contacts without a wider access plan.
objectives: Identify a recruitment channel that favors familiar contacts without a wider access plan.
Revise an unclear posting description while preserving approved qualifications.
Separate broader outreach from a promise of preference or selection.
takeaways: Word of mouth can supplement outreach without becoming the whole recruitment strategy.
A clear description helps people judge whether the role fits their experience.
Publicity does not authorize changing posting or selection requirements.
lessons.statement: Broader outreach creates an opportunity to compete; it does not promise a hiring outcome.

image.caption: A clear opportunity description helps people understand the work and the approved application path.

intro.heading: Who can find and interpret the posting?
intro.body:
A team may share a vacancy through colleagues who know the agency well. That can bring useful applicants, but it can also reproduce the existing network. Qualified people outside it may never hear about the role or may be unable to interpret its internal terminology. Examine both discovery and understanding. A public posting can exist while the practical invitation reaches only people who already know someone inside.

Work through approved recruitment channels and the applicable posting requirements. Consider whether occupational networks, educational contacts, community partners, and other appropriate channels can distribute the same accurate information. The aim is an open opportunity for qualified applicants, not a promise that identity or connection will determine the result. Do not arrange a private shortcut for someone recruited through a favored contact.

Read the description as a person new to DHS. Acronyms, internal project names, and vague phrases such as “excellent fit” can obscure the duties. Explain what the role does and what capabilities the approved process will assess. Keep the formal requirements intact while improving surrounding language through the authorized review. A clearer description should neither conceal demanding responsibilities nor add intimidating qualifications that are not part of the posting.

Examine application access. A candidate may need assistance understanding the process or requesting accommodation. Provide the established contact and route requests to responsible staff; do not ask applicants to disclose medical information to the recruitment network. Do not assure them of a particular accommodation or individual result without authority. An accessible invitation includes a way to ask a question without being evaluated through an informal conversation.

Separate outreach activity from evidence about its effectiveness. The number of places a posting was shared is not proof that new candidates could use it. Review the process with HR using authorized information. Do not infer race, disability, or other identity from names or photographs to create your own recruitment report. A leader can identify which channels were used and which communication barriers were reported without guessing demographic characteristics.

inThisLesson: Examine reach beyond familiar contacts.
Explain the role without internal shorthand.
Keep one approved application path.
Review outreach without guessing applicant identities.
lessons.keyStatement: Communicate the same real opportunity clearly across a wider set of approved channels.

items.title: An invitation through colleagues
items.body: A colleague can help share an opportunity. The concern is reliance on that route alone or informal promises about who will be selected. Use the accurate posting and established application instructions. Personal familiarity should not become a requirement that was never announced.

items.title: A specialized network
items.body: An occupational or community partner can help reach people with relevant experience. Explain the duties and application process without implying that membership in the network guarantees preference. Keep questions and assistance within approved recruitment practices, and review whether other channels are also needed.

items.title: An unfamiliar process
items.body: Candidates new to state employment may not understand the steps, the qualifications, or how to request assistance. Clear instructions and the right contact can reduce that uncertainty. Avoid creating special assessment conversations outside the approved process simply because someone asks a thoughtful question.

tabs.label: Discovery
tabs.body: Discovery concerns who has a reasonable opportunity to encounter the posting. A manager’s network may reach capable people, but depending entirely on that network repeats its existing boundaries. Approved additional channels can broaden reach while distributing the same requirements. Record the channels used; do not infer that a larger contact list proves equal access.

tabs.label: Understanding
tabs.body: Understanding concerns what a reader can make of the opportunity. An external applicant may know the work but not a DSD acronym. Explain the task and formal requirements accurately so terminology does not become an unintended insider test. Plain wording improves information; it does not authorize removing a qualification or promising that everyone will qualify.

tabs.label: Access
tabs.body: Access concerns whether a person can use the application route and obtain appropriate assistance. A posting can be understandable yet point to an unusable process. Confirm the assistance contact and approved arrangement with responsible staff. Keep support requests out of informal applicant comparisons; neither the request nor its private details are evidence of job ability.

check.question: A vacancy is posted publicly but distributed only through the manager’s friends. What is the most useful improvement?
check.correct: Use approved additional channels to share the same accurate posting and application route, while keeping qualification and selection decisions consistent.
wrong: Promise applicants from a new channel that they will receive hiring preference.
Choose the manager’s acquaintance quickly because outreach takes time.
Guess applicants’ identities from their names to prove the contact list is diverse.
check.feedbackCorrect: The process gains reach without replacing job-related criteria or inventing an outcome promise.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Hiring preference cannot be promised merely because someone came through a new outreach channel. Choosing a friend quickly leaves the network barrier intact and may bypass the selection process. Guessing identity from names creates unreliable and inappropriate information. Broaden approved outreach while retaining accurate requirements and consistent assessment.

items.text: Approved partners share the same vacancy and application instructions.
The role is described only with internal acronyms.
A network contact is promised a job before assessment.
The posting gives the established assistance contact.
A candidate cannot tell which duties are central.
Applicants from one contact list are told they can skip the official process.

lessons.next: Next, compare applications using the criteria rather than the familiarity of their examples.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Alan posts a role supporting service guidance. His team circulates it among current contacts and says few outside candidates seem interested. An external partner explains that the title and internal acronyms make the work difficult to recognize. Alan can improve explanatory wording through HR and use additional approved distribution channels.
options: Keep the posting as written because outside applicants should already understand state terminology.
Promise the partner’s members priority to increase applications.
Clarify the tasks and application assistance, broaden approved distribution, and preserve the same selection criteria.
responses: Unexplained terminology can hide an otherwise relevant opportunity. Reviewing clarity does not remove professional expectations.
A recruitment channel is not an authorized preference rule. Do not promise a result.
This improves access to the opportunity while maintaining a consistent assessment process.

lessons.transfer: Review a public or practice posting. Identify one internal phrase and one additional approved outreach channel. How can you explain the role without changing its requirements?

move.control: You can improve clarity and approved outreach before treating limited response as lack of interest.
move.failure: The team interprets a narrow contact network as proof that few qualified people are available.
move.next: Confirm one recruitment communication and channel review with HR before the next posting closes.

lessons.title: Screen evidence with a consistent standard
lessons.summary: A screening decision should connect the application to approved criteria without giving familiar experience an unannounced advantage.
lessons.objective: Apply an approved criterion to two differently worded experience examples.
objectives: Apply an approved criterion to two differently worded experience examples.
Identify an unsupported inference in a screening note.
Explain how an ambiguity should be handled consistently through the authorized process.
takeaways: Equivalent capability can be described in unfamiliar language.
Do not infer motivation or ability from gaps, names, or writing style without job-related evidence.
Resolve ambiguity with the same authorized approach across candidates.
lessons.statement: Read for evidence of the criterion, not resemblance to the person the team knows.

image.caption: Screening notes should explain evidence against a criterion rather than personal impressions.

intro.heading: What does the application actually show?
intro.body:
Two candidates can describe similar work differently. An internal applicant may use the exact name of a DHS process. An external applicant may describe comparable responsibilities in another organization. Familiar terms make the first application easier to read, but that ease is not itself evidence of stronger capability. Ask whether the documented work demonstrates the approved requirement rather than whether the wording sounds like the agency.

Use the established screening criteria and authorized methods for clarification. Do not add a preference during screening because one example is appealing. If a criterion asks for experience analyzing policy, identify the analysis described: what information was reviewed, what choices were compared, and what result the applicant helped produce. Keep a concise note tied to that evidence. Do not write an inference about personality where the application supplies only a gap or an unfamiliar title.

Ambiguity requires consistency. A brief application may leave a required point unclear. Whether and how clarification is permitted depends on the hiring process. Consult HR rather than independently calling only the candidate you know. If additional information is allowed, use the authorized comparable approach. An informal conversation can create evidence that other candidates were not offered a chance to provide.

Check common shortcuts. A prestigious employer can indicate relevant experience but cannot substitute for examining the responsibility. A career interruption does not establish lack of commitment. An unfamiliar name or address is not evidence of communication ability, eligibility, or willingness to work. Screening should not turn identity assumptions into a prediction about job performance. If a formal eligibility question exists, the responsible office handles it through the established procedure.

Record what the process shows and what it does not. A person may fail to demonstrate a particular requirement in an application; that is different from declaring them incapable of the work in every setting. Keep real applicant records in approved systems, not course reflections. The quality of a screening process is visible in whether a screener can connect each outcome to the same criteria and the evidence used.

inThisLesson: Read different descriptions against one criterion.
Replace impressions with evidence notes.
Route ambiguity through a consistent method.
Keep private applicant information out of learning notes.
lessons.keyStatement: A screening note should allow another screener to follow the evidence and criterion.

items.title: A familiar organization
items.body: An employer’s name may prompt confidence because screeners know its reputation. Ask what the candidate actually did and whether that evidence meets the criterion. The same examination should apply to work in a less familiar setting. Reputation can guide a question; it should not silently replace the assessment.

items.title: A career gap
items.body: A gap in the timeline does not show why it occurred or whether the person meets a qualification. Avoid inventing a story about commitment or reliability. Focus on the relevant documented experience, and use authorized procedures for any legitimate clarification. Do not ask for personal medical or family information simply to explain the gap.

items.title: An unclear responsibility
items.body: If the application does not establish a required responsibility, note that uncertainty accurately. Consult the process owner about permitted clarification. The concern is not resolved by extending special help only to a familiar applicant or by inventing missing evidence for someone the manager prefers.

tabs.label: Criterion
tabs.body: The criterion is the approved requirement, not a new preference prompted by a particular resume. For example, comparing service information is different from having worked in one named DHS unit. State the requirement first so an unfamiliar work history can be considered on its substance. An added preference needs authorized review, not quiet use during screening.

tabs.label: Evidence
tabs.body: Evidence describes what the application actually establishes about the requirement. A different title may cover relevant responsibility, while a familiar title may reveal little about what the person did. Examine the permitted details and use the same approved clarification approach. Avoid filling gaps through reputation, personal acquaintance or unnecessary private information.

tabs.label: Outcome
tabs.body: The outcome explains the relationship between evidence and criterion. “Not demonstrated” is more precise than declaring someone incapable when the materials do not establish a requirement. Follow the authorized screening rules for uncertainty. A short rationale linked to the standard supports review; a confident unsupported judgment only conceals the missing evidence.

check.question: An external applicant describes work comparable to an internal process using a different title. What should the screener do?
check.correct: Examine the responsibilities against the approved criterion and use the same authorized clarification method, rather than treating unfamiliar terminology as lack of experience.
wrong: Reject the application because it does not use the exact DHS process name.
Assume all external work is equivalent without reading the details.
Call only the internal candidate to obtain extra evidence.
check.feedbackCorrect: The assessment focuses on capability and a consistent evidence approach, not the ease of recognizing familiar words.
check.feedbackIncorrect: An unfamiliar DHS process name does not establish missing capability; read the actual responsibilities. Conversely, calling all external experience equivalent ignores relevant differences. Offering only an internal candidate extra clarification creates unequal evidence opportunities. Compare permitted evidence with the criterion and use the authorized clarification method consistently.

items.text: The application describes comparing policy options against documented criteria.
A career gap means this person is not committed.
Only a familiar candidate received an informal clarification call.
The described responsibility demonstrates the stated writing requirement.
An unfamiliar surname means communication may be difficult.
A new preference was added after applications were reviewed.

lessons.next: Next, examine how interview evidence can either correct or repeat earlier assumptions.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Becca screens applications for an analyst role. A familiar applicant uses the exact agency term for policy review. Another describes comparing regional program options and writing recommendations under a different title. Another screener wants to mark the second application as unqualified because the internal term is missing. Becca has the approved criterion and access to HR process advice.
options: Assess the described responsibilities against the criterion and consult HR on any ambiguity, keeping the approach comparable.
Accept both applications without assessing the requirement.
Reject the external example and let the interview panel handle fairness later.
responses: This examines the evidence and protects consistent access to the next stage.
Fairness still requires an actual assessment of the approved qualification.
A biased screening outcome cannot be repaired for a candidate who never reaches the interview. Examine the evidence now.

lessons.transfer: Using two practice experience descriptions, write evidence notes against one criterion. What familiar wording might have influenced your first impression?

move.control: You can ask screeners to show the criterion and evidence for each screening conclusion.
move.failure: Unfamiliar experience is rejected while an internal label is treated as proof without examination.
move.next: Before screening begins, confirm the evidence-note and ambiguity approach with HR and the designated screeners.

lessons.title: Assess the answer rather than the presentation style
lessons.summary: Interview evidence is stronger when questions and ratings examine the actual capability instead of charisma, speed, or resemblance to the panel.
lessons.objective: Identify a style-based judgment that is not supported by a job-related rating standard.
objectives: Identify a style-based judgment that is not supported by a job-related rating standard.
Connect an interview question to a defined capability and acceptable evidence.
Explain why a consistent interview permits appropriate accommodation without changing the capability being assessed.
takeaways: A confident delivery is not automatically evidence of the required skill.
Comparable questions and rating standards need to be established before interviews.
Access arrangements do not justify a negative inference about a candidate.
lessons.statement: Ask what the answer demonstrates for the role before deciding how impressive the delivery felt.

image.caption: Interviewers can examine different answers against the same job-related standard.

intro.heading: Make the evidence visible
intro.body:
A panel may leave an interview saying that a candidate “felt ready.” Sometimes that impression rests on relevant examples. Sometimes it rests on fluent delivery, shared professional references, or the ease of conversation. The next question is what the answer demonstrated. If the role requires comparing evidence and explaining a recommendation, did the candidate describe those actions? A familiar communication style should not replace that examination.

Use the required approved interview approach for the position. Structure includes predetermined job-related questions and rating criteria. The statewide recruitment policy establishes covered requirements; HR confirms the applicable procedure. This lesson develops judgment within that process rather than authorizing a new assessment. Define what a satisfactory response would show before seeing who supplies it.

Consider an example question: “Describe how you compared two options when the evidence was incomplete.” Useful evidence might include identifying uncertainty, seeking relevant information, explaining trade-offs, and deciding on a review step. The answer need not describe the agency’s exact project to demonstrate those capabilities. Ask whether the rating distinguishes a supported recommendation from unsupported confidence. Do not require the candidate to repeat the panel’s preferred vocabulary unless that specific terminology is genuinely part of the approved requirement.

Consistency concerns the opportunity and standard, not the removal of access support. A candidate may use an approved accommodation that changes presentation conditions while preserving the capability being assessed. Route the request appropriately and keep medical information outside panel deliberations. Do not reduce a rating because an aid, pause, or adjusted format was used. If the requested arrangement raises an assessment question, HR and the responsible accommodation process handle it.

Panel members should record evidence soon enough to avoid replacing it with a memory of the person. Notes can describe the actions, reasoning and results in the answer. They should not describe irrelevant appearance or presumed identity. A structured process does not eliminate every bias, but it gives panel members a basis to notice when an impression is doing the work of a criterion.

inThisLesson: Connect a question to capability.
Describe acceptable evidence before the interview.
Separate delivery impressions from rated content.
Preserve approved access arrangements and privacy.
lessons.keyStatement: Rate the capability the answer demonstrates under the approved standard.

items.title: A polished delivery
items.body: A well-organized answer may demonstrate a relevant communication skill. It should still be examined against the criterion rather than rewarded simply for confidence. An answer that sounds polished but does not explain the reasoning may supply less evidence than a slower account with clear trade-offs and follow-through.

items.title: An unfamiliar example
items.body: A candidate may describe a situation outside DHS that demonstrates the required capability. Read the action and result, not only the organization’s name. If the panel needs agency-specific knowledge, that requirement and rating should be explicit, approved and assessed comparably.

items.title: An accommodation request
items.body: Use the responsible process and preserve confidentiality. The panel should receive the information needed to conduct the interview, not unrelated medical history. Discuss any effect on the assessment with HR rather than improvising a penalty or treating the request as evidence of poor suitability.

tabs.label: Question
tabs.body: The question should elicit evidence of the actual work. Asking how someone compared uncertain service options can reveal reasoning; asking whether they are naturally confident mostly invites self-description. Use approved questions and context consistently. Friendly conversation does not justify adding an unrelated personal inquiry that never appeared in the assessment plan.

tabs.label: Evidence
tabs.body: The answer supplies the candidate’s actions, considerations and results. A permitted neutral probe can clarify an unclear example; a leading suggestion supplies missing content. If one candidate is coached toward “gather evidence first,” the panel may be scoring its own advice. Assess what candidates demonstrate through the approved opportunity, not what interviewers put into their answers.

tabs.label: Rating
tabs.body: The rating connects the demonstrated evidence to the predetermined standard. Speaking pace or resemblance to a panel member’s career can influence impressions without establishing the capability. When communication is genuinely part of the job, use its defined criteria. Explain the judgment through relevant evidence and address uncertainty through the authorized review process.

check.question: A candidate speaks slowly but describes clear evidence gathering and trade-offs. Another is fluent but gives no reasoning. What should guide the rating?
check.correct: The approved capability and evidence standard, with relevant communication criteria assessed as defined rather than assumed from speed or confidence.
wrong: The faster speaker should always score higher.
The candidate whose example resembles the panel’s own career should win.
An accommodation or pause should automatically lower a rating.
check.feedbackCorrect: This preserves the distinction between relevant assessed communication and unsupported style preferences.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Fast speech can be fluent without showing reasoning. A familiar career story may feel persuasive but does not satisfy an unstated criterion. An accommodation or pause is not itself evidence of weak capability. Rate the actions and reasoning under the approved standard, including relevant communication criteria only as defined.

items.text: The candidate explains how conflicting evidence affected the recommendation.
The candidate was quiet, so leadership must be weak.
A request to change the interview format for access.
The answer identifies an uncertainty and a follow-up review.
The candidate used an unfamiliar phrase, so teamwork will be poor.
A proposed question asks for private medical history.

lessons.next: Next, compare ratings without letting the first confident opinion set the group’s conclusion.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Omar’s panel interviews two candidates for a process-improvement role. One confidently says they “always find the right answer” but offers little detail. Another pauses and describes how they revised a plan after finding missing evidence. A panel member calls the second candidate less professional. The approved rating assesses analysis and communication through specific evidence.
scenario.prompt: What should Omar ask the panel to do?
options: Follow the most confident panel member’s impression.
Explain each rating against the approved evidence standards and separate any relevant communication evidence from unsupported style judgments.
Discard communication as a criterion in every interview.
responses: Confidence in the room does not establish a job-related assessment. Ask for evidence.
This allows the panel to examine the actual criteria without treating a delivery preference as an automatic result.
Communication may be relevant to the role. The concern is assessing it fairly through defined standards rather than removing it universally.

lessons.transfer: Write one practice answer summary and a rating rationale tied to the approved capability. Which adjectives would you replace with evidence?

move.control: You can require evidence-based ratings and refer access or question concerns to responsible staff.
move.failure: Charisma or familiarity determines the outcome while the rating standard remains unused.
move.next: Practice rating one practice answer with the panel before interviews and resolve differences in the standard with HR.

lessons.title: Deliberate without moving the goalposts
lessons.summary: A selection discussion should reconcile evidence and approved criteria rather than invent a new reason to favor a candidate.
lessons.objective: Identify an unannounced criterion introduced during deliberation.
objectives: Identify an unannounced criterion introduced during deliberation.
Use independent evidence notes to examine a rating disagreement.
Develop a response to a conflict of interest or suspected discrimination concern through the responsible process.
takeaways: A final discussion should use the same approved criteria as the assessment.
Differences in ratings can prompt examination rather than pressure for immediate consensus.
Formal concerns require the designated route, not a private deal to keep the process moving.
lessons.statement: The last discussion should explain the evidence, not rewrite the definition of success.

image.caption: A deliberate review makes differences in ratings discussable without letting status determine the answer.

intro.heading: What changed between the criteria and the decision?
intro.body:
After interviews, a panel may discover that its preferred candidate is not strongest under the documented ratings. Someone proposes “overall fit” as the deciding factor. The phrase may describe a genuine concern or hide a new preference. Ask what it means, whether it was approved as a criterion, and what evidence supports it. Do not let the final discussion become a place to add requirements candidates had no opportunity to address.

Independent notes help preserve judgment before group influence. A senior member may state a strong preference early, making other panel members doubt evidence they had recorded. Review the assessment approach with HR, and use a deliberation process that lets each member explain their relevant evidence. The objective is not to force every rating to be identical. It is to understand why they differ and apply the standard consistently.

Examine discrepancies at the level of the answer. One panel member may have heard a clear example of follow-through; another may have focused on a weak description of the outcome. Compare the documented evidence and the rating anchor. If the anchor is ambiguous, use the authorized process for resolution rather than changing it casually for the favored candidate. Keep a record of the rationale that can be reviewed appropriately.

Personal relationships and other conflicts need the established disclosure route. A panel member who knows an applicant may offer relevant authorized information or may have a conflict affecting their role. The supervisor should consult the responsible hiring process, not simply instruct that person to “stay objective” and proceed. If discriminatory reasoning or another serious concern appears, address it through HR or the appropriate equal-opportunity office. Do not resolve it by trading votes or deleting an uncomfortable note.

Keep lawful appointment requirements distinct from the panel’s learning exercise. Veterans’ preference, collective bargaining provisions, classification, and other applicable rules are not optional criteria that a group can waive through consensus. The course does not decide how they apply to a real vacancy. A clear selection recommendation explains the job-related evidence and the authorized process followed, without pretending that a learning checklist certifies legal compliance.

inThisLesson: Look for new criteria at the final discussion.
Examine independent evidence and rating differences.
Use conflict and concern routes.
Separate panel judgment from formal appointment requirements.
lessons.keyStatement: Do not add a new standard because the approved one points away from the person someone prefers.

items.title: “They are a better fit”
items.body: Ask for the capability, approved criterion, and evidence behind the phrase. A panel may mean collaboration or adaptability, which can be relevant if defined. It may also mean similarity or personal comfort. Do not accept the vague label as an extra criterion candidates could not anticipate.

items.title: The ratings differ
items.body: Invite panel members to explain the evidence, then examine the same rating anchor. A difference is not proof that someone is biased, and majority agreement does not automatically resolve it. Use the authorized deliberation method and retain a rationale for a changed rating or final recommendation.

items.title: A serious concern arises
items.body: Use the designated process for a conflict, discriminatory statement, or procedural irregularity. Preserve relevant records and privacy. Continuing quickly does not erase the concern. The supervisor should seek the responsible advice rather than making a private arrangement intended to avoid review.

tabs.heading: Three parts of the selection account

tabs.label: Evidence
tabs.body: The evidence account should show relevant actions and results, including any limitations. “I can picture them here” describes comfort, not performance under a criterion. Returning to what the assessment actually established helps members compare answers without importing private identity information or relying on a colleague’s reputation to fill a gap.

tabs.label: Criteria
tabs.body: Criteria provide the stable basis for comparison. If a preferred candidate is weaker under the stated standard, adding “similar to our team” moves the goalposts. Identify the proposed change and raise it through HR review. Agreement among panel members cannot turn an unannounced preference into a sound retrospective assessment.

tabs.label: Procedure
tabs.body: Procedure determines how a recommendation becomes an authorized decision. Panel members may assess evidence and advise, while other roles handle required review and selection authority. Keep those responsibilities visible. A unanimous panel conclusion is useful information, but it cannot waive a governing rule, remove required records or confer powers the panel does not hold.

check.question: A panel adds “similar to our current team” after interviews because its preferred candidate did not lead under the criteria. What should the leader do?
check.correct: Challenge the unannounced preference, return to approved job-related evidence, and seek HR guidance on the procedural concern.
wrong: Accept the preference because the team knows who will be comfortable.
Change the ratings to match the desired result.
Delete the original criteria so the recommendation appears consistent.
check.feedbackCorrect: This addresses the shifted standard and preserves a reviewable process.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Team comfort cannot validate a new resemblance preference after interviews. Altering ratings to obtain a desired result loses the evidence basis, and deleting criteria hides the procedural concern. Preserve the record, return to the approved job-related standards and seek the responsible HR review rather than manufacturing consistency.

items.text: Panel members compare the same answer with the approved rating anchor.
A new preferred-employer criterion appears after interviews.
A panel member has an undisclosed personal relationship with an applicant.
A rating change is explained with documented response evidence.
“Someone like us” becomes the final deciding factor.
A panel member proposes ignoring an applicable appointment requirement.

lessons.next: Next, review the completed process for lessons and improvements without exposing applicant information.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Soren’s panel has documented ratings. A senior panel member prefers a former colleague and says the person is “a natural fit.” Another candidate showed stronger evidence against the criteria. The senior panel member proposes adding agency familiarity at the last meeting. Soren also learns the relationship was not discussed when the panel was formed.
options: Return to the approved evidence, seek HR advice on the new criterion and relationship, and preserve the assessment record.
Select the former colleague because the senior panel member can guarantee success.
Raise the colleague’s ratings and remove the notes describing the change.
responses: This addresses both evidence and process rather than accusing motives or treating familiarity as authority.
A personal assurance cannot replace the documented standard and applicable hiring process.
Altering the record to fit a preference conceals the problem and undermines review.

lessons.transfer: Use a practice panel discussion to identify one shifted standard and write the evidence question a chair should ask. Do not include actual candidate records.

move.control: You can protect the approved criteria and use the responsible review route when concerns appear.
move.failure: The final discussion introduces familiarity as a criterion and edits the record to support a desired outcome.
move.next: Agree with HR on a deliberation method and concern-escalation route before the first interview.

lessons.title: Review the process and carry improvements forward
lessons.summary: A completed hire is a point to examine access and decision quality, not proof that the process was fair in every step.
lessons.objective: Select process-review questions that examine reach, access, screening and evidence.
objectives: Select process-review questions that examine reach, access, screening and evidence.
Distinguish an authorized aggregate review from individual identity guessing or public applicant disclosure.
Assign one improvement before the next vacancy rather than tailoring it retroactively.
takeaways: A successful hire does not explain which qualified candidates never reached assessment.
Review the process using authorized information and responsible privacy practices.
Make improvements prospective and carry them into the next approved plan.
lessons.statement: Learn from the process without turning applicants into examples or rewriting the completed decision.

image.caption: A process review can identify where access and evidence should improve in the next cycle.

intro.heading: What would we change before doing it again?
intro.body:
The new employee may perform well, and the team may consider the hiring process successful. That result matters, but it does not answer every question about access or selection. A qualified person may have been discouraged by unclear requirements, unable to use a response method, or screened out because unfamiliar experience was misread. A process review asks where the opportunity and evidence could improve without assuming that any particular result proves the whole process fair or unfair.

Review the stages rather than beginning with a desired demographic explanation. Which outreach channels were used? Which questions or access problems were reported? Were screening notes linked to approved criteria? Did the interview ratings use evidence? Were conflicts and formal requirements handled through the proper routes? These questions can reveal process issues without guessing anyone’s identity or motive.

Use only authorized information for demographic or aggregate analysis. Work with HR and data-responsible staff on definitions, access, and privacy. Small numbers, missing data, and differences in roles can make conclusions uncertain. A disparity in an authorized report can identify a question for investigation; it does not by itself establish unlawful discrimination or explain the cause. A lack of data is not proof that no barrier occurred.

Separate improvement from retroactive tailoring. If the review identifies an unclear qualification, revise the next draft through authorized approval rather than pretending it was not used in the completed process. If a procedural concern might affect a real decision, refer it promptly to the responsible office. A course reflection is not the venue to decide a remedy or investigate a complaint.

Choose one improvement with an owner and timing. It may be clarifying a task description, widening approved outreach, improving evidence notes, or rehearsing a rating standard. Record why the change addresses the identified concern and how it will be checked. Staff should develop and carry the improvement, using consultant guidance for reflection and feedback. The next hiring plan should show the change before candidates apply, so fairness is designed into the opportunity rather than explained afterward.

inThisLesson: Review stages rather than only outcomes.
Use authorized evidence and privacy practices.
Separate uncertainty from causal conclusions.
Assign a prospective improvement and review point.
lessons.keyStatement: Improve the next approved process using evidence from this one, while routing real concerns appropriately.

items.title: Access and reach
items.body: Examine which channels were used and which practical barriers were reported. Distinguish publicity from usable access. If evidence about a missing perspective is unavailable, record the gap. Do not infer a population’s interest from the absence of applications in a narrow recruitment effort.

items.title: Evidence and consistency
items.body: Review whether criteria were confirmed before use and whether screening and interview notes supported the outcomes. Look for ambiguities that could be improved in the next plan. Preserve the original records and use authorized review methods; do not revise them to make the completed process look cleaner.

items.title: Improvement and responsibility
items.body: Select a specific change and confirm the appropriate authority. Assign who prepares it, who approves it, and when its effect will be checked. Consultant feedback can help the team examine assumptions, but it does not replace HR review or the leader’s responsibility for the hiring work.

tabs.label: A finding
tabs.body: A finding states what the review can establish, such as unequal clarification opportunities documented in the record. Describe its scope and evidence rather than turning it into a broad allegation. A specific finding gives the responsible office something to examine and gives the next process owner a concrete practice to improve.

tabs.label: A question
tabs.body: A question marks what remains unknown. A progression-rate difference may warrant examination, but limited data alone does not establish its cause. Missing information is not proof of fairness either. Identify what authorized evidence and qualified review could clarify the pattern, while avoiding private identity guesses or disclosure of individual employment histories.

tabs.label: An action
tabs.body: An action connects a finding to an appropriate response. Clarifying a future question set may be within a process-improvement plan; handling an actual selection concern requires the responsible formal route. Name the owner and next check. Do not imply that a prospective improvement automatically supplies an individual remedy or closes an existing concern.

check.question: An authorized review finds a difference in progression rates across groups, but the data is limited. What is the strongest next step?
check.correct: Treat it as a question for careful authorized investigation, examine process evidence and data limits, and avoid declaring a cause or absence of concern prematurely.
wrong: Declare discrimination proven from the rate difference alone.
Ignore the difference because the successful hire is doing well.
Guess identities from names to fill missing data quickly.
check.feedbackCorrect: This preserves the concern and the uncertainty while keeping analysis within responsible information practices.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A limited rate difference does not alone prove discrimination, but the successful hire’s performance does not explain away a process pattern. Guessing identity cannot responsibly repair missing data. State the concern and limits, examine authorized process evidence and refer for appropriate review without declaring either a cause or an absence of concern.

items.text: The screeners used two different clarification approaches.
Why did people withdraw before the interview?
Confirm one comparable clarification procedure before the next vacancy.
A posting relied on unexplained internal terms.
Did the recruitment channels reach qualified people outside current networks?
Review the next posting language with HR before announcement.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to review one approved hiring plan. The related structured-interview course develops questions, panel preparation and ratings in greater detail.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Petra reviews a completed analyst hiring process. The new employee is performing well. The record also shows unfamiliar experience was interpreted differently by two screeners, and only one candidate received clarification. Petra can bring the concern to HR and improve the next process, but she cannot decide an individual remedy or alter original records.
options: Close the review because the employee is successful.
Preserve the records, refer the actual procedural concern to HR, and prepare a consistent screening improvement for the next approved process.
Change the old screening notes so the process appears uniform.
responses: The outcome does not remove the documented concern about opportunity and consistency.
This distinguishes responsible handling of the current concern from prospective learning and improvement.
Rewriting records conceals the issue rather than correcting the process.

lessons.transfer: Write one de-identified process finding, one unanswered question, and one prospective improvement. Which role has authority over each?

move.control: You can arrange a responsible process review and carry a specific improvement into the next hiring plan.
move.failure: A successful hire ends all scrutiny, or the review edits records instead of addressing the concern.
move.next: After one hiring cycle, review a specific access or assessment concern with HR and assign a prospective improvement before the next posting.

jobAid.subtitle: An evidence-and-access review across the hiring process.
remember: Confirm approved criteria before reviewing candidates.
Compare capability through relevant evidence, not familiarity.
Use HR and responsible offices for actual decisions and concerns.

sections.heading: Before posting
items: Connect each requirement to a task and evidence.
Keep the criteria independent of a favored applicant.
Confirm applicable posting, classification and appointment procedures.

sections.heading: Recruitment and screening
items: Use approved channels beyond familiar contacts.
Clarify internal terms without independently changing requirements.
Apply the same approved criteria and clarification approach.
Write evidence notes rather than identity or motivation assumptions.

sections.heading: Interview and deliberation
items: Use the approved questions and rating standards.
Arrange access through the responsible process.
Assess answer evidence rather than charisma or speed.
Challenge new criteria introduced after interviews.
Disclose conflicts and route serious concerns appropriately.

sections.heading: Review and improve
items: Preserve original applicant and decision records in approved systems.
Keep real applicant information out of course reflections.
Use authorized aggregate evidence and state its limits.
Refer actual procedural concerns to HR.
Assign one prospective improvement with an owner and review point.
